messages.content:
You are verifying one structured PFAS study evidence record against the
complete source evidence cited by that record.

You receive:
1. the review task and task-specific extraction objective;
2. the held-out anchor identifiers;
3. one extracted evidence record; and
4. the complete source chunks or inspected source-page text referenced by the
   record.

Judge only source support and transcription. Do not reward usefulness,
verbosity, or agreement with general background knowledge.

Assess every substantive populated source-dependent field against only its
attached field-level locators. Do not create separate assessments for locator
arrays, record IDs, or formatting metadata:
- supported: the cited evidence directly supports the field and its material
  qualifiers;
- partially_supported: the core statement is supported but a material
  qualifier, condition, denominator, or scope is missing;
- unsupported: the cited evidence does not establish the field;
- contradicted: the cited evidence directly conflicts with the field.

For quantitative_findings, value must contain an actual number, censored or
approximate number, range, or explicit ND/not-detected result. A unit-shaped
string such as "nmol/L" in value with an empty unit is a unit error even when
the source mentions that concentration scale. Do not silently reinterpret one
schema field as another. Confirm that value matches value_form; explanatory
text and uncertainty belong in qualifiers.

Classify endpoint_type from the measured basis, not the source's terminology.
Parent-compound loss alone is not destruction; phase transfer is not
degradation; inorganic fluoride release or fluorine-balance closure establishes
defluorination but not mineralization. Mineralization requires direct
carbon-fate evidence such as measured CO2/inorganic carbon or a carbon balance.
If an author calls defluorination mineralization without that evidence, retain
the author phrase only as reported_term and mark endpoint_type=mineralization
unsupported with error_type=endpoint_classification.

Comparability is an analyst-derived judgment. Do not require the source to
state the comparability conclusion verbatim. Instead, judge whether its status
and reason follow conservatively from supported cited fields for matrix, PFAS
scope, scale, conditions, endpoint, unit, and denominator.

An author_reported limitation requires direct source support. A
design_inferred limitation is supported when it follows necessarily from
cited design facts; absence from the supplied packet is not a study
limitation.

Classify errors as numeric_transcription, unit, qualifier,
endpoint_classification, source_attribution, other, or none. A record is usable
only if its source identity, matrix, treatment, endpoints, and quantitative
findings are not unsupported or contradicted in a way that would mislead
  synthesis. A usable record can still contain non-core fields that synthesis
must exclude according to their field assessments.

For metric consistency, always emit separate assessments with these exact
field-path forms when the corresponding item exists:
- `quantitative_findings[i].value`;
- `quantitative_findings[i].unit`;
- `operating_conditions[i].value`;
- `operating_conditions[i].unit`;
- `endpoints[i].endpoint_type`; and
- `comparability.status`.

Other substantive fields may be assessed individually or as a whole object,
but do not omit these required assessment types and do not emit a required
field path more than once.

Report anchor_exclusion_violation=true if the source resolves to any held-out
anchor DOI, URL, exact title, or corpus source.

Return one JSON object that follows the supplied verification schema exactly.

field_assessments.reason: The record DOI/URL exactly matches the DOI given in the source metadata: 10.1016/j.watres.2021.117781 / https://doi.org/10.1016/j.watres.2021.117781.

Endpoint is regeneration recovery defined as mass of PFAS released to aqueous phase vs mass preloaded on resins (S08-E02). This is a phase-transfer separation of PFAS from resin to regenerant, so classification as a separation endpoint is appropriate.

S08-E02 defines regeneration recoveries as “mass of PFAS released to the aqueous phase vs. mass of PFAS preloaded on the resins” and S08-E04/S08-E07 discuss variation with brine concentration and resin type, matching the interpretation text.
S08-E02 refers to “regeneration recoveries,” the term used in the record.

S08-E02 states: “the resins used in our regeneration experiments had < 1% capacity consumed by PFAS,” directly supporting low PFAS loading. The added interpretive clause that “regeneration performance was evaluated under low PFAS loading conditions” is reasonable but is not explicitly framed by the authors as a study limitation, so the limitation is only partially supported as author-reported.

Design-inferred limitation: S08-E02 notes only the top five PS-DVB resins (A592E, PFA694E, DOWEX1, TAN1, IRA910) were used for regeneration; S08-E04 and S08-E07 describe laboratory tests with simple chloride salt brines. It reasonably follows that results may not generalize to other resin chemistries or full-scale systems.

S08-E02 describes regeneration recoveries as mass of PFAS released to the aqueous phase vs mass preloaded on IX resins using regenerants; S08-E04 discusses brine concentrations. This supports the matrix description of PFAS-loaded IX resins contacted with aqueous regenerant solutions.

S08-E02 lists A592E, PFA694E, DOWEX1, TAN1, and IRA910 as the top five PS-DVB resins used for regeneration tests; S08-E07 and S08-E08 describe gel-type vs macroporous and PFAS-specific vs other strong-base anion resins, matching the summarized description.
This field is descriptive (resin types) and correctly has no unit (null), consistent with the qualitative nature of the information in S08-E02/S08-E07/S08-E08.
S08-E04 states “brine concentrations ranging from 0.01% to 10%…,” which matches the recorded range 0.01–10.
S08-E04 reports concentrations in %, and representing this as % (w/v) is a reasonable and standard interpretation for salt brines; no conflicting unit information is given.
S08-E05 specifies: “The brine was NH4Cl for A592E, PFA694E, and TAN1, and NaCl for DOWEX1 and IRA910,” consistent with the recorded brine types at the 10% condition described in S08-E04/S08-E07.
Brine type is categorical, so a null unit is appropriate and consistent with the qualitative description in S08-E05.
S08-E02 states: “the resins used in our regeneration experiments had < 1% capacity consumed by PFAS,” which matches the recorded initial PFAS loading value of <1% of resin capacity.
The text in S08-E02 is in percent of resin capacity; using “% of resin capacity” as the unit is consistent and appropriate.

S08-E01 and S08-E08 discuss short-chain PFCA and PFECA and note that regeneration is higher for short-chain PFCA and PFECA; S08-E01/E03 list multiple PFAS classes (PFBA, PFBS, PFEA, zwitterions, FASAA). Together they support that mixtures of various PFAS, including short-chain PFCA, PFECA, and other emerging PFAS, were studied.

S08-E04 reports “the median average recoveries for A592E, PFA694E, DOWEX1, TAN1, and IRA910 increased to 8%, 4%, 5%, 16%, and 22%, respectively, by 10% brine,” so the value 8 for A592E is correctly transcribed as an exact numeric percentage.
S08-E04 gives the recovery values as percentages; the unit “%” is correct.
S08-E04 lists the median average recovery for PFA694E as 4% at 10% brine, matching the value 4 recorded.
Recoveries are reported in percent in S08-E04; unit “%” is appropriate.
S08-E04 lists the median average recovery for DOWEX1 as 5% at 10% brine, matching the value 5 recorded.
Recoveries are reported as percentages in S08-E04; unit “%” is correct.
S08-E04 lists the median average recovery for TAN1 as 16% at 10% brine, matching the value 16 recorded.
Recoveries are expressed as percentages in S08-E04; unit “%” is correct.
S08-E04 lists the median average recovery for IRA910 as 22% at 10% brine, matching the value 22 recorded.
Recoveries are expressed in percent in S08-E04; unit “%” is correct.

S08-E02 defines regeneration recoveries as mass of PFAS released to the aqueous phase; S08-E04/S08-E07 describe use of chloride brines as regenerants. It logically follows that PFAS are transferred into brine solutions, creating PFAS-laden brine as a secondary residual, consistent with the design-inferred statement.

The work is clearly described as controlled regeneration tests (figures, varying brine concentrations, resin screening) in Water Research, indicating laboratory scale. S08-E02 notes practical application for drinking water treatment, supporting the description of lab tests for drinking water treatment applications.

S08-E02 identifies the five PS-DVB resins used for regeneration; S08-E04 describes brine concentrations from 0.01% to 10% and use of chloride brines; S08-E07 emphasizes 10% simple chloride salts without organic solvents as the most reasonable option for regenerating PFAS-loaded PS-DVB resins. This supports the treatment description of regenerating PFAS-loaded PS-DVB IX resins with inorganic salt brines of varying concentration.

All quantitative findings share: same endpoint definition (regeneration recovery = mass released to aqueous phase vs mass preloaded, S08-E02), same matrix (PFAS-loaded PS-DVB resins), same unit and denominator (percent recovery, S08-E04), and same key operating condition (10% chloride brine; S08-E04, S08-E05, S08-E07). Differences in resin type and PFAS mixture mean comparability requires conditions, so “comparable_with_conditions” is a justified analyst judgment.

S08-E02 defines the regeneration recovery basis (mass to aqueous vs mass preloaded). S08-E04 provides the specific median recoveries at 10% brine for each PS-DVB resin. S08-E05/S08-E07 define the brine type and note the use of 10% simple chloride salts as the optimal/practical condition. These collectively support the stated comparability rationale about common endpoint and conditions with differences in resin type and PFAS composition.

result.record_usable_rationale: Core elements—source identity, matrix, treatment description, regeneration endpoint definition, operating conditions, and all quantitative regeneration recoveries with correct units and magnitudes—are supported by the cited text. The only minor issue is an interpretive framing of an author-reported limitation, which does not affect use of the quantitative data for synthesis.
